title: The Sleeper's Author: Chicopee Falls, Looking Backward, and the Movement That Came Out of a Book
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Baptist House at Chicopee Falls

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the minister's son is born
stops.date_confidence: attested; birthdate confirmed twice, by Wikipedia and by the inscription on the family obelisk at Fairview Cemetery. Coordinate marks the village centre, since the Church Street house was not built until 1852 and he was not born in it
stops.campa: In the mill village of Chicopee Falls, Rufus King Bellamy, Baptist minister, and Maria Louisa Putnam Bellamy have a son on the twenty-sixth of March and name him Edward. The father descends from Joseph Bellamy, the Great Awakening theologian. The mother is a minister's daughter herself; her own father left his Salem pulpit rather than give up his Freemasonry. The boy arrives in a house where the doctrine of election is argued at table and the factory hands walk past the door twice a day, going to the cotton mills and the rifle works on the river.
suggested_refs: The village of Chicopee Falls in 1850, cotton mills and the Ames works on the Chicopee River
sources: Waymarking WMRK6V, Fairview Cemetery obelisk inscription

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the village school
stops.date_confidence: attested that he attended the public school of Chicopee Falls; the year is a reasonable estimate only, and no teacher, curriculum, or schoolhouse building is named in any accessible source. Coordinate is the village centre, not a structure
stops.campa: He goes to the public school of the village. No teacher's name and no schoolhouse survives in the record, only the village itself: water-driven mills filling with Irish labor, a landscape of paid hands and owners that he will still be describing forty years later when he sets a coach on a sandy road and harnesses the masses to it. His mother's Calvinism runs alongside the schoolroom. In that doctrine judgment is real, and a wrong arrangement of the world is something a person will answer for.
stops.quote: The nation does not maim and slaughter its workmen by thousands, as did the private capitalists and corporations of your day.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Project Gutenberg e-text #624
suggested_refs: The public schools of Chicopee Falls in the 1850s and 1860s
sources: Inference from family background is marked [R] in the report and is not asserted as causation here

stops.name: West Point, the physical examination
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and outcome by three independent sources; month unknown, defaulted to January. Upgraded from the gathering lens, which had tagged it tradition. Coordinate corrected: the submitted 42.3608, -73.9721 lay 107 km north of the Academy, in Columbia County
stops.campa: At seventeen he travels down the Hudson to the United States Military Academy and sits the entrance examination. He fails it, not on the books but on the body: rejected for physical frailty. Elizabeth Sadler records the rejection in the New England Quarterly, and the reference literature agrees on the year. The career of arms closes before it opens. He goes home to Chicopee Falls. It is the first time an institution measures his body and turns him away on the measurement.
suggested_refs: Elizabeth Sadler, 'One Book's Influence,' New England Quarterly 17 (1944)
sources: Elizabeth Sadler, 'One Book's Influence,' New England Quarterly 17 (1944)

stops.name: Union College, two semesters and no degree
stops.date_confidence: attested that he enrolled in 1867 and completed two semesters; the September start is conventional and not documented. Coordinate corrected to the Nott Memorial, which the gathering lens named but missed by about 285 m
stops.campa: He enrols at Union College in Schenectady and stays two semesters, taking no degree. Here he reads Herbert Spencer and the evolutionary social theorists, an exposure his biographers reach back for whenever they need to explain the later utopia; that reading is tradition rather than document. The coordinate marks the Nott Memorial at the middle of the old campus, not a room he is known to have used. He leaves for Europe without finishing. In his generation that is common and carries no disgrace with it.
suggested_refs: The Nott Memorial and the Ramee campus of Union College, Schenectady
sources: Spencer reading is general biographical tradition, not confirmed from a primary document this session

segments.name: Dresden, the Law Office, and Newspaper Row

stops.name: Dresden, the year abroad
stops.date_confidence: attested that he spent 1868 to 1869 in Germany with a cousin; the city of Dresden is given by Encyclopedia.com and is not in the Wikipedia spine, so the city level is one source deep. Month unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: With a cousin he crosses to Europe and settles in Dresden, capital of the Kingdom of Saxony, staying through 1869. The court city is one thing and the industrial quarters are another, and the distance between them is the lesson the biographical tradition says he carried home. He is nineteen. He has now seen a European poverty organised on a different plan from the American poverty of his own mill village, and found that the different plan produced poverty all the same.
suggested_refs: Dresden and its industrial suburbs under the Kingdom of Saxony, 1868-1869
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Bellamy House' (Bowman chronology: 'from 1868 to 1869 he lived in Germany with a cousin')

stops.name: Springfield, admitted to the bar
stops.date_confidence: attested as June 1871 by Encyclopedia.com, corroborated by the swiftpapers biography. This corrects Wikipedia, which dates the law study to the 'late 1860s'. Day unknown, defaulted to 01; coordinate is Court Square, the firm's numbered address not established
stops.campa: He reads law in the offices of a Springfield firm and is admitted to the bar in June 1871. He takes one case. Then he stops, and never returns to the profession. The common summary that he studied law but never practised is not quite right, because he practised once, and once was all of it. The law leaves him no living. It leaves him a working vocabulary: contract, obligation, the enforceable claim, the difference between a right a man holds and a favour he must ask for.
suggested_refs: The Hampden County bar rolls for June 1871
sources: swiftpapers biography of Bellamy (aggregator, corroboration only)

stops.name: Newspaper Row, the New York Evening Post
stops.date_confidence: attested that he took a position with the New York Evening Post in 1871; month unknown, defaulted to January. No numbered address for his desk was found, so the coordinate marks the Park Row newspaper district
stops.campa: He goes to New York and takes a place on the Evening Post, in the Park Row district where the city's papers stand shoulder to shoulder across from City Hall. No numbered address for his desk survives in the accessible sources; the coordinate marks the Row. He is twenty-one, writing to a daily deadline in the largest newspaper market in the country, learning the trade he will use for the next twenty years and the pace his lungs will shortly refuse to keep.
suggested_refs: Newspaper Row, Park Row, Manhattan, in the early 1870s
sources: Exact building address in Newspaper Row not confirmed this session

stops.name: Springfield, the Union and the return to Massachusetts
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1872 and for the role; month unknown, defaulted to January. The paper's numbered address is not fixed in accessible sources, so the coordinate marks Court Square in the city centre
stops.campa: Within a year he leaves New York for Massachusetts and joins the Springfield Union as editorial writer and literary critic. He keeps at the Union, contrary to the tidy version of his life that has him quitting journalism in 1878, until 1881: reviews, editorials, the weekly column of a working newspaperman. The move brings him back within an hour of the family house at Chicopee Falls, and every address he holds after this one stands inside that hour.
suggested_refs: The Springfield Union in the 1870s, Court Square, Springfield

stops.name: Springfield, tuberculosis at twenty-five
stops.date_confidence: attested that the disease appeared at about age 25; the year 1875 is derived from that age and no month or day is recorded. Coordinate is the city he was working in, not a clinical record
stops.campa: At about twenty-five the disease arrives: tuberculosis, the century's ordinary killer of young men who work indoors. It will recede and return for twenty-three years and then finish him. From this point his working life is organised around it. Daily journalism is a physical trade, hours on the street and hours at the desk, and he begins the slow negotiation away from it, toward work he can do sitting down, at home, on his own hours, in a house he does not have to leave in bad weather.
suggested_refs: Consumption in the industrial Connecticut valley, 1870s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Bellamy' ('At age 25, he developed tuberculosis')

stops.name: Port of San Francisco, the passage west
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction only. No ticket, passenger list, or letter places Bellamy in San Francisco. The stop is inferred from standard 1870s trans-Pacific steamship routing and should be read as routing, not evidence. Month and day unknown
stops.campa: Steamers for Honolulu leave from San Francisco, and any passage booked from Massachusetts to the Kingdom of Hawaii runs across the continent and out through this port. No ticket, no passenger list, and no letter places him on the Embarcadero. The stop stands here as routing and not as evidence: the standard way west in the 1870s, taken by a consumptive travelling for his lungs, with the whole width of the country already behind him and the ocean still to cross.
suggested_refs: Pacific Mail steamship service, San Francisco to Honolulu, 1870s
sources: Inferred from standard 1870s trans-Pacific steamship routing via San Francisco; no direct documentary source for Bellamy's transit located this session

stops.name: Honolulu, the year in the Kingdom of Hawaii
stops.date_confidence: attested that he spent a year in the Hawaiian Islands, 1877 to 1878; month of arrival unknown, defaulted to January. No lodging, street, or Honolulu address is named in any accessible source, so the coordinate marks the historic downtown waterfront
stops.campa: He spends a year in the Kingdom of Hawaii, based at Honolulu, on the standard prescription of the age: warm air for a diseased lung. No lodging house and no street is named in anything reachable, so the coordinate marks the old downtown by the harbour. He comes back in 1878 improved and not cured, which is the only outcome that prescription ever produced. He is twenty-eight, a newspaperman with a bad chest, and he has not yet published a book. From here he arranges his working life so that the work comes to him rather than he to it.
suggested_refs: Honolulu waterfront under Kalakaua, 1877-1878
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Bellamy' ('spent a year in the Hawaiian Islands (1877 to 1878)')
Specific Honolulu address not identified in accessible sources

stops.name: Nantucket, Six to One
stops.date_confidence: publication in 1878 attested; whether Bellamy ever visited Nantucket is undocumented, and the stop is a reconstruction from the novel's setting. Month unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: His first novel, Six to One: A Nantucket Idyl, is published in 1878 and set on this island. Whether he walked the place or built it out of reading and other people's descriptions is not established by anything reachable, and the stop is a reconstruction from the setting rather than a documented journey. The title counts the island's women against its men, the arithmetic the whaling trade left behind. The book is a slight one. It establishes only that he intends to be a novelist.
suggested_refs: Six to One: A Nantucket Idyl (New York, 1878)
sources: No direct evidence of a visit to Nantucket located this session

stops.name: Great Barrington, the Berkshire Courier serial
stops.date_confidence: attested that The Duke of Stockbridge ran as a serial in the Berkshire Courier of Great Barrington in 1879; the specific months are not established, so the date defaults to January. Coordinate marks the town, no printing-office address confirmed
stops.campa: The Duke of Stockbridge, a romance of Shays' Rebellion, runs as a serial through 1879 in the Berkshire Courier at Great Barrington. It is finished work, not a fragment. The frequent description of it as an unfinished novel comes from the 1900 book, which his cousin edited so heavily that the Harvard edition of 1962 went back to this serial text instead. Arthur Morgan held that the novel's town is modelled on Chicopee, not on Stockbridge. Bellamy is writing about armed debtors shutting a courthouse, nine years before he writes about the courthouse abolished.
suggested_refs: The Berkshire Courier, Great Barrington, 1879 serial run of The Duke of Stockbridge
Harvard/Belknap John Harvard Library edition, ed. Joseph Schiffman (1962)
sources: Harvard/Belknap 1962 edition of The Duke of Stockbridge, ed. Joseph Schiffman

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the Penny News printed in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Springfield Penny News was founded in 1880 by Edward and his brother Charles and that it began publication in the Chicopee Falls house; month unknown, defaulted to January. This corrects the gathering lens, which placed the paper in a downtown Springfield office and said it folded
stops.campa: Edward and his brother Charles found the Springfield Penny News, a tri-weekly, and it begins publication in the family house at Chicopee Falls before it has an office of its own. It does not fold. It becomes the Springfield Daily News and outlives them both. The paper is a cheap sheet for people who cannot afford the Union, which is a version at one cent of the argument he will shortly make at book length. He is running a newspaper out of the room where he writes his novels.
suggested_refs: The Springfield Penny News, later the Springfield Daily News, founded 1880
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Bellamy House' (citing Morgan p. 127: 'it began publication in the house')

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, Dr. Heidenhoff's Process
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January. That the book was written in the Church Street house is inference from his settled residence there from 1872
stops.campa: In the same year he publishes Dr. Heidenhoff's Process, a short novel about a machine that erases a memory and, with it, the guilt attached to the memory. A woman ruined by one night is offered surgical forgetting; the cure turns out to be a dream. It sells poorly. The method is already the method of the utopia: take one intolerable feature of ordinary life, invent the machine that removes it, and then examine what is left of the person. He will run it again on a whole country.
suggested_refs: Dr. Heidenhoff's Process (New York, 1880)

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the marriage to Emma Sanderson
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, unresolved. The geography lens gave 31 May 1882; genealogical aggregations of the Hampden County records (Familypedia, WikiTree) give 30 May 1882 at Chicopee. Both are weak sources. The 30th is used here and the disagreement is not settled
stops.campa: He marries Emma Augusta Sanderson at Chicopee. She has been a ward of his father's household since 1874, raised in these rooms nearly as a sister. Two children follow, a son Paul and a daughter Marion. Genealogical compilations of the Hampden County records give the thirtieth of May; other summaries give the thirty-first, and the day is not settled. They live in the Church Street house, with one interval next door in 1886 while a second child is coming, and return when Rufus Bellamy dies that November.

The Fairview Cemetery obelisk, which dates Emma S. Bellamy 12 February 1861 to 4 September 1956

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, Miss Ludington's Sister
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1884 by the Library of Congress, archive.org, and WorldCat, and by 1884 on both the title and copyright pages. Wikipedia's 1885 is an error, and the gathering lens contradicted itself, its chronology giving 1885 and its geography 1884. Month unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Miss Ludington's Sister: A Romance of Immortality is published at Boston by James R. Osgood and Company, with 1884 on the title page and on the copyright page. An old woman believes her young self survives somewhere as a separate soul, and a medium produces her. The book asks whether a person's earlier self is a different person. Julian West will answer that question with his own body four years from now. Wikipedia dates this novel to 1885; the Library of Congress and the printed book both say 1884.

segments.name: The Book and the Decade That Was Ready For It

stops.name: Roxbury, the cousin in the pulpit
stops.date_confidence: attested in francis_bellamy.journey.json for the pastorate and its dates; pin inherited byte-identical from that file. The pairing of the two cousins' arguments is stated as juxtaposition, not as documented collaboration
stops.campa: Four miles from where Looking Backward will be published, Francis Bellamy, Edward's first cousin, takes the pulpit of the Dearborn Street Baptist Church in Roxbury and preaches that the distribution of economic resources is a religious question. He holds this pulpit five years. The two cousins are working the same argument from opposite ends of the trade, one from a Baptist pulpit in Boston, one from a novelist's desk in a mill village, both of them out of the same New England Baptist family.
suggested_refs: Dearborn Street Baptist Church, Roxbury, Francis Bellamy's pastorate 1885-1890

stops.name: New York Harbor, Liberty Enlightening the World
stops.date_confidence: dedication date and pin attested in francis_bellamy.journey.json and inherited byte-identical. The extension of that file's civic-symbol framing to Edward Bellamy is my own bracketing and is not stated in any corpus file
stops.campa: Liberty Enlightening the World is dedicated in New York Harbor on the twenty-eighth of October, two years before Looking Backward is published. The decade is manufacturing civic symbols at speed. A colossus goes up in the harbour. Francis Bellamy will write a pledge for schoolchildren six years from now, and his cousin's novel hands the republic a picture of itself in the year 2000. The atlas records this dedication in the francis_bellamy file inside exactly that frame. Edward Bellamy is at his desk in Chicopee Falls, three years into the book.
suggested_refs: The dedication of the Statue of Liberty, 28 October 1886

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the manuscript finished
stops.date_confidence: attested that he planned the novel through the 1880s, completed it in 1887, and submitted it to Benjamin Ticknor; no month is given for completion, so the date defaults to January
stops.campa: He completes Looking Backward: 2000-1887 in the Church Street house, having planned it across the decade. Julian West, a Boston gentleman of 1887, goes to sleep in a sealed underground chamber and wakes in the year 2000 into a Boston with no money, no advertising, no lawyers, no servants, and no poor. The nation has absorbed the corporations and become the single employer of everybody. He sends the manuscript to the Boston publisher Benjamin Ticknor.
stops.quote: A man's natural endowments, mental and physical, determine what he can work at most profitably to the nation and most satisfactorily to himself.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Project Gutenberg e-text #624
suggested_refs: The Edward Bellamy House, 91-93 Church Street, where Looking Backward was written

stops.name: 211 Tremont Street, Ticknor publishes the first edition
stops.date_confidence: January 1888 first edition attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the gathering lens placed the firm at the Old Corner Bookstore, conflating Benjamin Ticknor's Ticknor and Company (211 Tremont Street, 1885-1889) with the older Ticknor and Fields, which had merged into Houghton in 1878
stops.campa: Ticknor and Company releases the first edition in January. The firm is Benjamin Ticknor's, formed in 1885 out of the second J. R. Osgood house, and it works from 211 Tremont Street; it is not the Ticknor and Fields of the Old Corner Bookstore, which had gone into Houghton ten years earlier. Sales are modest and local. The book that will be the third best-selling American novel of the century starts as a slow-moving title in a Boston publisher's winter list.
stops.quote: By way of attempting to give the reader some general impression of the way people lived together in those days, and especially of the relations of the rich and poor to one another, perhaps I cannot do better than to compare society as it then was to a prodigious coach which the masses of humanity were harnessed to and dragged toilsomely along a very hilly and sandy road.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Ch. 1, Project Gutenberg e-text #624
suggested_refs: Ticknor and Company, 211 Tremont Street, Boston, 1885-1889
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Bellamy' (third best-selling American novel of the century)

stops.name: Tremont Temple, the First Nationalist Club
stops.date_confidence: October 1888 founding attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01. THE VENUE IS NOT DOCUMENTED: Tremont Temple is offered as a plausible reform hall and could not be confirmed this session. Pin inherited byte-identical from francis_bellamy.journey.json
stops.campa: Readers of the novel organise the First Nationalist Club of Boston in October, the first of some hundred and sixty-two clubs that will form across the country to argue for the nationalisation of industry. Bellamy does not found it. He is adopted by it, having written the book and then stood aside while readers built the organisation. Tremont Temple is given here as a plausible hall for such a gathering, the reform meeting place of the city, and not as a documented address; the venue was not confirmed from any source reached this session.
stops.quote: As no such thing as the labor question is known nowadays, replied Dr. Leete, and there is no way in which it could arise, I suppose we may claim to have solved it.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Ch. 5, Project Gutenberg e-text #624

stops.name: Tremont Temple, the Society of Christian Socialists
stops.date_confidence: attested in francis_bellamy.journey.json, which names Edward Bellamy in its own stop text; date and pin inherited byte-identical
stops.campa: Four months later, in the same hall, Francis Bellamy helps found the Society of Christian Socialists. His file in the atlas names the connection outright: his cousin Edward has published Looking Backward the year before and has a movement of his own. The same stop sets William Morris preaching the identical reform in London through the identical decade. A pulpit in Boston, a novel out of a mill village, and a hand press on the Thames are running one argument about who owns the work.

stops.name: Park Street, the Houghton Mifflin reissue
stops.date_confidence: September 1889 reissue attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is Houghton Mifflin's historic Park Street address and is not independently confirmed for this transaction. Note that the two sales-rank claims in the sources, third best-selling of the century and second in early sales, are not identical and are not reconciled here
stops.campa: Houghton Mifflin reissues Looking Backward from Boston in September with minor revisions, and the book detonates. Sales pass four hundred thousand copies by 1897 and five hundred and thirty-two thousand by the middle of 1939; the United Kingdom takes more than two hundred and thirty-five thousand between 1890 and 1935. Contemporary observers rank its early sales second in the century behind Uncle Tom's Cabin. Elsewhere it is called the third best-selling American novel of the century. Both rankings are in the sources and neither is adjudicated here.
stops.quote: That it was equally the duty of every citizen to contribute his quota of industrial or intellectual services to the maintenance of the nation was equally evident, though it was not until the nation became the employer of labor that citizens were able to render this sort of service with any pretense either of universality or equity.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Ch. 6, Project Gutenberg e-text #624

stops.name: London, the Fabian Essays
stops.date_confidence: date and pin attested in annie_besant.journey.json and inherited byte-identical. The parallel to the Nationalist Clubs is inference: no textual link between Besant and Bellamy exists in either corpus file or in anything reached this session
stops.campa: Fabian Essays in Socialism appears in London in December, the same season the Nationalist Clubs are multiplying across America. Annie Besant has a chapter in it. Two gradualisms, neither Marxist, neither expecting a barricade: the British one arguing its way through committees, the American one arguing its way through a novel about a man asleep. No letter connects Besant to Bellamy in the atlas or anywhere reached. The parallel is a parallel and is offered here as nothing more than that.

stops.name: Kelmscott House, News from Nowhere begins
stops.date_confidence: date and pin attested in william_morris.journey.json and inherited byte-identical. That file states the utopia content and does NOT name Bellamy as its provocation; the review and rebuttal are documented outside the atlas, not in it
stops.campa: William Morris begins serialising News from Nowhere in Commonweal from his house on the Hammersmith river bank, having reviewed Looking Backward in the same paper the year before and disliked it thoroughly. Morris answers Bellamy's nation-as-corporation with a moneyless, prisonless England of handwork and small fellowship. The atlas file for Morris records the utopia and never names Bellamy as its cause. The provocation is well documented outside the atlas and is claimed here on that footing.
stops.quote: On the contrary, there was absolutely no violence. The change had been long foreseen. Public opinion had become fully ripe for it, and the whole mass of the people was behind it.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Ch. 5, Project Gutenberg e-text #624

stops.name: Boston, The New Nation is founded
stops.date_confidence: founding year attested; month unknown, defaulted to January. The paper's street address is not established in accessible sources, so the coordinate marks the downtown Boston publishing district
stops.campa: He founds and edits The New Nation, a weekly published from Boston to argue the Nationalist programme in the press, and commutes to it from Chicopee Falls. No street address is established in anything reachable; the coordinate marks the downtown publishing district. He is a novelist who has become the editor of a party organ, which is the conversion the Britannica notice will describe twenty years later, from the far side of his death, in a single clause.

stops.name: The United States, one hundred and sixty-two clubs
stops.date_confidence: the count of approximately 162 clubs by 1891 is attested; the coordinate is the geographic centre of the contiguous states, used as an explicit marker for a national fact with no single place, and is NOT a location Bellamy occupied. Month unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: By this year some hundred and sixty-two Nationalist Clubs are counted across the country. Bellamy works them toward united action with the People's Party, pressing for planks the Nationalists can own. The coordinate is the geographic centre of the contiguous states, a marker for a national count and not a place he stood in. Within a year the club activists are largely absorbed into the party apparatus, and the movement's separate name starts going out of use in the very season of its greatest reach.
stops.quote: Society is so constituted that there is absolutely no way in which an official, however ill-disposed, could possibly make any profit for himself or any one else by a misuse of his power.

stops.name: Shanghai, the Chinese serial
stops.date_confidence: serialisation across 1891 and 1892 attested; no month is given, so the date defaults to January 1891. Coordinate marks Shanghai, the city of publication of Wanguo Gongbao, since no editorial address is fixed in accessible sources
stops.campa: The missionary Timothy Richard produces an abridged Chinese Looking Backward, serialised through 1891 and 1892 in Wanguo Gongbao under the title Huitou kan jilue, later issued as Bainian Yi Jiao, A Sleep of 100 Years. It is described as the first Western science fiction published in Qing China. The periodical was published at Shanghai; the coordinate marks the city, no editorial address being fixed anywhere reachable. A Boston sleeper wakes into a Chinese reform argument.

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the Nationalist years at home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That he kept his primary residence at Chicopee Falls through the New Nation years is the residence pattern given by general biographical tradition and is not itemised in a single accessible source. Date is a mid-period marker, not an event
stops.campa: Through the run of The New Nation he keeps his residence at Church Street, writing pamphlets and answering the movement's correspondence between trips to Boston. The health that failed him at twenty-five does not improve under this schedule. He is forty-one at the paper's founding and organising a national movement out of a house in a mill village, with one bad lung, on the strength of a book he wrote in the front room of it. The village has not changed. The mills still run. The clubs corresponding with him number in the scores and none of them is on this street.
stops.quote: The principle is that no man's work ought to be, on the whole, harder for him than any other man's for him, the workers themselves to be the judges.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Ch. 7, Project Gutenberg e-text #624

stops.name: Sofia, the adaptation Bellamy approved
stops.date_confidence: attested that Iliya Yovchev produced an adapted rather than literal Bulgarian version relocating the setting to Sofia, with Bellamy's personal approval; the sources treat it as a separate category from the standard 1892 Bulgarian translation. Month unknown, defaulted to January. Coordinate is the city the adaptation moved the book into, not a printing address
stops.campa: Iliya Yovchev renders the novel into Bulgarian not as a translation but as an adaptation, moving Julian West's Boston to Sofia. Bellamy approves it personally. A direct Bulgarian translation also appears in 1892, and the sources keep the two in separate categories. Elsewhere the Russian edition is banned outright by the Tsar's censors, who read the book the same way and drew the opposite conclusion from it. The count of thirteen languages sometimes given for the book is not supported by the source that carries it.

stops.date_confidence: dedication date and pin attested in francis_bellamy.journey.json and inherited byte-identical. The extension to Edward Bellamy's Nationalist movement in the same season is my own bracketing and is not stated in any corpus file
stops.campa: The World's Columbian Exposition is dedicated at Jackson Park on the twenty-first of October, the four hundredth Columbus Day, and opens the following spring as a white plaster city with its own power plant and no visible poverty in it. The same season, out of the Youth's Companion office in Boston, Francis Bellamy's school ceremony and its pledge go to the nation's classrooms. Edward Bellamy's clubs are arguing for the thing itself while the fair puts up the picture of it in staff and paint.

stops.name: Boston, The New Nation ceases
stops.date_confidence: attested that the paper ceased in 1894 owing to financial difficulties; no month is given, so the date defaults to January. Same district-level coordinate as the founding stop, the address being unestablished
stops.campa: The paper closes in 1894 for want of money, four years after it opened. The closure is the practical end of the Nationalist Clubs as an organised force. What survives is the novel, which keeps selling in several languages while the organisation built on it disperses into the People's Party and then out of it again. He is forty-four and has spent the peak years of his reputation editing a weekly instead of writing books. Subscribers who want the whole programme are still buying it in the novel the paper was founded to advertise.
stops.quote: The nation, that is to say, organized as the one great business corporation in which all other corporations were absorbed; it became the one capitalist in the place of all other capitalists, the sole employer, the final monopoly in which all previous and lesser monopolies were swallowed up, a monopoly in the profits and economies of which all citizens shared.
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Looking Backward: 2000-1887 (1888), Ch. 5, Project Gutenberg e-text #624

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, Equality
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month unknown, defaulted to January. That it was written at the Church Street house follows from his settled residence there and is not separately documented
stops.campa: He publishes Equality, the sequel, written at Church Street as the tuberculosis closes in. It answers the critics of Looking Backward at length and extends the argument into the vote for women, reproductive freedom, the treatment of animals, and the keeping of wilderness. It never approaches the reach of the first book. It is the fuller statement and the smaller readership. What the first book left the reader to work out for himself, this one sets down at length.
stops.quote: How can men be free who must ask the right to labor and to live from their fellow-men and seek their bread from the hands of others?
stops.quote_source: Edward Bellamy, Equality (1897), Ch. 3, Project Gutenberg e-text #7303

stops.name: Denver, the western cure that may not have happened
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, unresolved. Some biographical accounts have Bellamy travelling to Colorado in his last months for a climate cure; Wikipedia's summary describes his death at Chicopee Falls and mentions no such journey. Nothing reached this session settles it. Date is a marker for the disputed window, not an arrival
stops.campa: Some accounts have him travelling west to Colorado in the last months, seeking dry air as he once sought the warm air of Honolulu. Other summaries keep him at Chicopee Falls throughout the final year and mention no journey at all. Nothing reachable settles it. The stop stands here as a contradiction rather than a fact. A disagreement between sources is part of the record, and it is left visible on the map rather than quietly decided in one direction or the other.

stops.campa: He dies in the Church Street house on the twenty-second of May, of the tuberculosis he had carried twenty-three years, forty-eight years old. He has outlived his movement by four years and his sales are still climbing. Julian West slept a hundred and thirteen years into a finished commonwealth. His author gets ten years from the book to the grave, long enough to watch the clubs form, the party absorb them, the paper fail, and the novel go on selling in languages he cannot read.

stops.name: Co-op City, Bellamy Loop
stops.date_confidence: attested that the street was named in July 1967; day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: A street in the northeast Bronx is named for him in July, inside Co-op City, a limited-equity housing cooperative of more than fifteen thousand apartments raised on a drained marsh. Toronto has a Bellamy Road as well. Neither is a monument in the ordinary sense, and neither carries a plaque explaining itself. A cooperative housing development that names a loop of its own roadway after the author of Looking Backward is doing something closer to a citation than to a statue: the residents hold their apartments in common and drive home along his name.

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the house made a landmark
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the coordinate published by the landmark listing itself
stops.campa: On the eleventh of November the house at 91-93 Church Street, built in 1852, is designated a National Historic Landmark. He lived in it from infancy, left it for Union College and New York, and made it his settled home again from 1872 until his death, with three intervals elsewhere. Looking Backward was written in it and the Penny News was first printed in it. The listing fixes the coordinate at 42.1561 north, 72.5841 west, which is the figure used throughout this file.

stops.name: Chicopee Falls, the Memorial Association takes the house
stops.date_confidence: acquisition year attested; month unknown, defaulted to January. The restoration is dated only to the 1970s and 1980s in the source
stops.campa: The Edward Bellamy Memorial Association acquires the house in 1974 and restores it across the two following decades. Part of the building is operated as a museum and the rest is rented out, the rent keeping the museum open. The arrangement would not have struck the man who wrote in it as ironic. The house pays for its own public use out of its own tenancy. It is the only building anywhere that holds both his name and his furniture, and visitors are shown the front room where Looking Backward was written.

stops.name: Emerson College, the musical telephone
stops.date_confidence: premiere year and venue attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 01
stops.campa: A century after the first edition, Roger Lee Hall's one-act musical play Bellamy's Musical Telephone premieres at Emerson College in Boston. The title takes the novel's most domestic invention: music piped into every room by wire, on demand, at any hour of the day or night. Mack Reynolds had already rewritten the book in 1974 as Looking Backward from the Year 2000, resetting the sleeper's wake in a future further off again. The nationalised industry never arrived. The music arrived exactly as written, into every room, on demand, and nobody who has it thinks of the man who described it first.
suggested_refs: Roger Lee Hall, Bellamy's Musical Telephone, premiered Emerson College, 1988
